newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank earnings seen extending growth trend.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank earnings seen extending growth trend.

text.p: U.S. bank earnings for the first quarter of 1997 are likely to be 10 to 12 percent higher than in the year-ago period, extending the trend of recent years.
"Top-line growth has slowed somewhat, but expense control is good and share buybacks are continuing," said Michael Mayo, an analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston.

An analyst who declined to be identifed said the handful of banks that reported first-quarter results by midday Wednesday had come in a little better than expected. "The key here seems to be really strong growth in fee income," the analyst said.

Ruchi Madan, a regional bank analyst at Prudential Securities, wrote in a report last week that the quarter's earnings reports should "confirm investors' positive fundamental outlook on the group." Overall, earnings per share are expected to rise 11 percent from the 1996 first quarter, the analyst said.
Madan said the reports were expected to show slower loan growth, stable interest margins, good fee income growth, modest expense growth and share repurchases by most companies.
In a resarch report last week, Brown Brothers Harriman analyst Nancy Bush said she expected "a continuation of the steady trends which we have seen for the past year or so."

Touching on one of the more controversial subjects in banking -- credit cards -- Bush wrote: "Our talks do not indicate that there is any lurking disaster on the credit quality front, but there is no relief in sight either -- just the continued negative creep as the consumer bankruptcy issue continues to simmer."
The loss rate on U.S. credit cards has been inching up for about a year, causing that segment of the business to be less profitaible.

Referring to credit cards, Gerard Klauer Mattison analyst Geroge Salem said, "It's a business that is in its own little world and fortunately not large enough to spoil the earnings stream of too many banks."
Salem, who tracks a mixture of money center banks and the bigger regionals, expects median earnings per share growth of 13 percent compared with the year-ago quarter.

He said the main influences on the earnings were healthy loan growth, particularly in the consumer sector, flat or slightly higher interest margins, solid trading revenue and modest non-interest income growth. He also cited expenses that were rising moderately and heavy stock buybacks for most banks.

Thomas McCandless, an analyst at NatWest Securities, took a somewhat different view of bank earnings, arguing that on a sequential quarter-to-quarter basis, pre-tax profits were growing in a range of three percent to four percent for the industry as a whole. He said if that kind of "linked quarter" growth persisted for two more quarters, widespread expectations of 1997 earnings growth of 11 to 12 percent may be too aggressive.

McCandless said two factors were at work. One is modest pressure on revenue and expenses in most categories, and the other is the difficult comparisons with 1996, which was a very good year for bank profits, he said.
McCandless said many banks have been depending on share repurchases to boost earnings per share in the double digits..

Some analysts have questioned whether share repurchases are a good use of a bank's excess capital, considering that bank stocks reached all-time highs earlier this year and fewer shares can be bought with the same amount of dollars. More recently, stock prices have retreated amid higher interest rates, although the analysts say higher rates will not hurt earnings of many banks.

The week beginning April 14 promises to be a heavy period for bank earnings, with NationsBank Corp expected to report on Monday, and Chase Manhattan Corp, Citicorp and Wells Fargo and Co among those expected Tuesday.
